hook: You spent 40 minutes picking a lunch spot. Was that door locked?
title: One-Way vs Two-Way Doors

game.prompt: If this goes wrong, can you walk back through the door?

items.text: Trying a new gym class this week
items.why: Hate it? Don't go next week. Cheap to undo, so decide fast.
Hard and painful to reverse. This one deserves slow thinking.

items.text: Picking a paint color for your room
items.why: Paint is cheap. A weekend fixes a bad call.

items.text: Lending all your savings to a friend's 'sure thing'
items.why: Money lent is hard to get back, and so is the friendship. Slow down here.

items.text: Testing a new morning routine for a week
items.why: A one-week experiment is the definition of reversible.

items.text: Saying something cruel in an argument
items.why: Words can be forgiven, but rarely unsaid. Pause before this door.

insight: Most choices are two-way doors: if they go wrong, you can step back. Save your slow, careful thinking for the few doors that lock behind you.
model: Ask 'Can I undo this?' Reversible: decide fast and learn. Irreversible: slow down.
try_today: Pick one choice you've been stalling on. If it's reversible, decide it in the next 5 minutes and treat it as a test.
try_team: List 5 choices your team, class or family keeps putting off. Vote: one-way or two-way door? Decide every two-way door before you leave the room.

hook: Do you treat a menu like a marriage? Let's see where you land.
title: How You Weigh Small Choices

game.right: Fast on small, slow on big

questions.q: Choosing a show to watch tonight, I usually…

options.label: Scroll for 20+ minutes and feel unsure
Narrow it to two, then pick
Pick one in a couple of minutes; I can switch

questions.q: Picking a birthday card for a friend, I…

options.label: Read most of the rack and still doubt my pick
Check a few, then go with one
Grab one that feels right and write a good message

questions.q: When a small choice turns out wrong, I…

options.label: Feel annoyed for a day, then let it go

questions.q: When buying something with free returns, I…

options.label: Read a few reviews, then buy
Buy the good-enough one and test it

zones.label: Today: over-deliberating
zones.text: Today your answers give small choices big-choice energy. That's tiring. Try a deadline for reversible picks and save your care for the big ones.

zones.label: Today: mixed
zones.text: Your answers today are mixed: some small choices get sorted fast, others eat your time. Asking 'Can I undo this?' tips them the right way.

zones.label: Today: sorting doors
zones.text: Your answers today move fast where it's safe and slow where it matters. Keep checking that 'fast' never sneaks onto a one-way door.

insight: Good deciders match speed to stakes. Barry Schwartz linked always hunting for the best option ('maximizing') to lower satisfaction, but later studies are mixed.
model: Match your decision speed to how reversible the choice is, not how anxious it makes you.
try_today: Set a 2-minute timer for your next small choice (food, show, outfit). When it rings, pick and don't look back.

source.work: Amazon shareholder letter (2015); The Paradox of Choice (2004)

try_team: Before your next group choice (a film, a trip, a project name), ask: can we undo it? If yes, set a 3-minute limit, pick, and move on.

hook: You're 80, in a rocking chair. Which choice still stings?
title: The 80-Year-Old Test

game.prompt: Imagine looking back from age 80. In studies of regret, which do most people say hurts longer: the risks they took that failed, or the chances they never took?
game.reveal: Over a lifetime, most people regret the chances they never took. Picked failed risks? That's true in the short run: fresh mistakes sting most. But they fade, while 'what if' stays open (Gilovich & Medvec, 1995).

insight: Failed tries hurt, then fade: you learn and move on. Untaken chances stay open as 'what if'. It's a lens for close calls, not a license for reckless bets.
model: From age 80, inaction usually hurts longer than a failed try. Let that tip close calls toward action.
try_today: Write down one thing you'd regret never trying. Then write the smallest first step you could take this week.

source.work: The experience of regret (Psychological Review, 1995); The Power of Regret (2022)

try_team: Each person finishes 'At 80, I'd regret our group never trying…' (club, class, family, team). Pick one and plan its first small step together.

hook: The 80-year-old test can be hijacked. Can you spot when?
title: Regret Test, Used Well

steps.scenario: An old friend you drifted from pops up on your feed. Messaging after 3 years feels awkward. Use the 80-year-old test. You…

options.text: Send one line: 'Saw this and thought of you'
options.feedback: Yes. The awkward bit lasts a minute. In Daniel Pink's big regret survey, lost friendships were one of the four most common kinds of regret.

options.text: Wait for them to message first
options.feedback: Very common, and they're probably waiting too. Looking back from 80, the unsent message is the one that tends to linger.

options.text: Leave it. If it mattered, it would have lasted
options.feedback: Friendships often fade from drift, not because they didn't matter. A short message is a cheap, two-way door.

steps.scenario: A mate says: 'Put all your savings into this new crypto coin. At 80 you'll regret missing out!' Does the test say yes?

options.text: No. That's fear of missing out using the test's name
options.feedback: Right. The test tips close calls toward trying. It can't turn a bet you can't afford to lose into a good one. All your savings is a one-way door.

options.text: Yes. Regrets about not acting last longest
options.feedback: Tempting logic, but that research is about chances people wished they'd tried, not bets that wiped them out. Losing your savings is a regret too.

options.text: Never take risks, then there's nothing to regret
options.feedback: Sounds safe, but from 80, a life with no tries is the regret people describe most. The skill is sizing the risk, not avoiding all of it.

insight: Regrets about not acting tend to last longer than regrets about acting (Gilovich & Medvec). But the test is for meaningful tries you can afford, not all-in bets.
model: Ask 'Will I regret not trying?' then 'Can I survive it failing?' Two yeses: go.
try_today: Message one person you've drifted from. Keep it to one line, like 'Saw this and thought of you.'
try_team: Everyone writes one 'I wish we'd tried…' for your group. Sort them: cheap to try, or a one-way door? Plan the cheapest one this month.

source.work: The experience of regret (Psychological Review, 1995); The Power of Regret (2022)

hook: Your plan already failed. It's a year from now. Why did it?
title: The Pre-Mortem

steps.scenario: Your group festival trip is in 2 months. Before you book anything, what's the smartest first move?

options.text: Picture it's after the trip and it was a disaster. List why.
options.feedback: Yes. That's a pre-mortem: 1) say the plan, 2) assume it already failed, 3) write reasons alone, 4) share, 5) fix the top risks. Step 2 is the key move.

options.text: Hype everyone up so nobody drops out
options.feedback: Energy helps, but it hides problems. Imagining the failure first brings them out while you can still fix them.

options.text: Wait and sort problems as they come
options.feedback: Common, but by then the easy fixes are gone. Naming risks now is cheaper.

steps.scenario: Your list: money ran out, someone's parents said no, tickets sold out, the tent broke. Which can you fix TODAY?

options.text: Someone's parents said no
options.feedback: One message tonight settles it. Fix the cheap, fast risks first.

options.text: Money ran out
options.feedback: Worth planning, but saving takes weeks. A budget chat is a good next step after the quick wins.

options.text: The tent broke
options.feedback: Good catch, but that's a check for the week before, not today.

insight: The key move is assuming it already failed: that frees people to name risks. Imagining an event as done helps people find more reasons for it (Mitchell et al., 1989).
model: Pretend it already failed, then ask why. Fix those reasons before you start.
try_today: Take one plan for this week. Write 'It failed because…' three times. Fix the easiest reason now.

source.work: Back to the Future: Temporal Perspective in the Explanation of Events (1989); Performing a Project Premortem (Harvard Business Review, 2007)

try_team: Next planning meeting or family trip chat: 5 minutes, everyone silently writes 'It failed because…', then read them out. Fix the top two risks first.

hook: Coin flip: win 100 or lose 60. Why do so many people say no?
title: Expected Value

game.question: Heads you win 100, tails you lose 60 (any currency). On average, how much is one flip worth?
game.explain: Expected value = chance × payoff, added up. 0.5 × 100 + 0.5 × (−60) = 50 − 30 = 20. Over many flips you'd average about +20 a flip.

insight: Losses tend to feel about 1.5–2× bigger than equal gains, so many people refuse bets like this that pay on average. Expected value shows the math under the feeling. One flip can still lose.
model: Odds × payoff, added up. Take bets with positive value that you can afford to lose.
try_today: Write two outcomes for one choice today, each with a rough chance and payoff. Multiply each pair and compare.

source.work: Pascal–Fermat letters (1654); Prospect Theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979); Thinking in Bets (2018)

try_team: Take one real group choice (a fundraiser, a trip, a new rule). Everyone guesses the chance and payoff of the best and worst case. Compare the numbers aloud.

from_source.quote: Let us weigh the gain and the loss in wagering that God is. Let us estimate these two chances.
from_source.cite: Blaise Pascal, Pensées, §233 (trans. W. F. Trotter, 1910)
from_source.next_read: Pensées §233, where Pascal applies the arithmetic of stakes to the question of God (read it as philosophy, not betting advice); then the 1654 Pascal–Fermat letters on fairly dividing an interrupted game.

hook: Bad outcome = bad decision? It feels that way. Here's why not.
title: Judge the Decision, Not the Dice

steps.scenario: Your friend spent weeks choosing a second-hand laptop: read reviews, asked someone who knows tech, tested it in person. A month later it dies. They say: 'I'm so stupid for buying it.' You reply…

options.text: "You decided well with what you knew. The outcome was bad luck."
options.feedback: Yes. Separating decision quality from outcome is the whole skill. It keeps them learning instead of blaming.

options.text: "Yeah, you should have seen it coming."
options.feedback: Hindsight makes the future look obvious. If no info pointed to it, the decision wasn't the problem.

options.text: "Never buy second-hand again."
options.feedback: Understandable instinct, but it learns the wrong lesson from one roll of the dice.

steps.scenario: Now flip it. Someone drives home after drinking and arrives safely. Good decision?

options.text: No. A good outcome doesn't fix a bad bet.
options.feedback: Right. The risk was real; they just got lucky. Luck doesn't make the decision wise.

options.text: Yes, nothing bad happened.
options.feedback: That's 'resulting': grading a choice by how it turned out. It teaches people to repeat lucky mistakes.

insight: Poker player Annie Duke calls it 'resulting': judging a choice only by how it turned out. Good choices sometimes lose; bad ones sometimes win. Judge the process.
model: Decision quality = what you knew and how you weighed it. Outcome = decision + luck.
try_today: Pick one past choice you regret. Ask: given what I knew then, was it reasonable? Write one sentence answering.
try_team: After a game, test or project, review one call in two columns: 'what we knew then' and 'what luck did'. Praise good process, even when it lost.

hook: Every yes has a hidden price. Quick: would you buy these?
title: What Is Not Seen

game.prompt: New trainers you love cost £60. Option A: buy them. Option B: keep the £60 for other things you want (tickets, food with friends, saving). Which do you pick?
game.reveal: No wrong answer. But in one study, just naming option B cut buyers from 75% to 55% (Frederick et al., 2009); later replications found a smaller effect. Bastiat's point, 1850: the cost you see is the price; the cost you don't see is everything else that money could have been.

insight: Every yes is a no to something else: money, time, attention. Our minds rarely show what we give up unless someone names it. Bastiat called it 'what is not seen'.
model: The real price of a yes is the best thing it pushes out. Name it before you agree.
try_today: Before your next yes (a purchase, a meeting, an hour online), name what it pushes out. Then decide.

source.work: What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen (1850); Opportunity Cost Neglect (Journal of Consumer Research, 2009)

try_team: Spending a shared budget or Saturday? Before voting, each person names what a yes pushes out. Decide only after the trade-offs are said aloud.

from_source.quote: the first only is immediate; it manifests itself simultaneously with its cause—it is seen. The others unfold in succession—they are not seen
from_source.cite: Frédéric Bastiat, That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen (1850), opening paragraph; 19th-century English translation
from_source.next_read: Bastiat, That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen, introduction and ch. 1 'The Broken Window'

hook: A free ticket. What did it really cost? 1 in 5 economists got it.
title: The Free Ticket Puzzle

game.question: You win a free ticket to Band A (you can't sell it). Same night, Band B costs £40, and seeing them is worth £50 to you. You go to Band A. What did you give up?
game.explain: £10. Going to A means giving up B. Seeing B was worth £50 to you but would have cost £40, so you give up £50 − £40 = £10 of value. When 199 economists got this puzzle (with 0, 10, 40 or 50 as options), only about 22% picked 10 (Ferraro & Taylor, 2005).

insight: Opportunity cost is the value of the best thing you give up, minus what it would have cost you. Even experts skip it. Some argue the puzzle's wording is unclear, so hold it lightly.
model: 'Free' isn't free: the cost is the best option you give up, minus its own price.
try_today: Pick one 'free' plan this week. Write what you'll miss to do it, and decide if it still wins.
try_team: Pose the ticket puzzle to your group and compare guesses. Then ask: what 'free' thing are we doing that quietly costs us a better option?

source.work: Do Economists Recognize an Opportunity Cost When They Sense One? (Topics in Economic Analysis & Policy, 2005)

hook: Pick one topic you give advice on. Are you inside your circle?
title: Circle of Competence

questions.q: Think of one topic you give advice on. I've had real results in it, not just opinions.
I can explain where my knowledge on it stops.
People who know more than me would mostly agree with my advice.
I feel sure when I talk about it.
I'd make a big decision on it without asking anyone.
I often say 'I'm not sure' on this topic.

results.name: Outside both (early)
results.text: Today you rate both your track record and your confidence low on this topic: it's new to you, and you know it. That's honest. Learn from people with results, and keep decisions small and reversible.

C.name: Confidence ahead of proof
C.text: You rate your confidence ahead of your track record on this topic. That's a common gap, and it's where mistakes slip in. Before big calls, ask someone with results to check you.

K.name: Proof ahead of confidence
K.text: You rate your track record above your confidence on this topic. Humility is good, but your knowledge could help others. Share it, and say where it ends.

CK.name: Inside the circle
CK.text: You rate your confidence and your proof about level on this topic. Your job now is guarding the border: notice when a question drifts past what you've tested.

insight: Warren Buffett's rule: the size of your circle matters less than knowing where its edge is. Socrates said wisdom starts with knowing what you don't know.
model: Know the edge of what you know. Act boldly inside it; ask, test, or pass outside it.
try_today: Write one topic where you're truly competent and one where you only feel confident. Ask an expert one question on the second.

source.work: Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter (1996); Plato, Apology

try_team: Each person names one topic they've truly tested and one they only feel sure about. Make a 'who to ask' list from it and use it next time you're stuck.

from_source.quote: he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.
from_source.next_read: Plato, Apology 20e–23c: the oracle at Delphi and Socrates' search for a wiser man

hook: You paid double for the worse weekend. Do you still go?
title: The Pricier, Worse Trip

game.prompt: You booked two weekend trips by mistake, same dates, no refunds. Trip A cost twice as much. Trip B is the one you'd enjoy more. You can only go on one. Which?
choices: Trip B, the one I'd enjoy more
game.reveal: Trip B. Both payments are gone whichever you pick, so only the weekend ahead counts. Yet when Arkes & Blumer (1985) gave students this puzzle, more than half chose the pricier trip they'd enjoy less.

insight: Money already spent can't be won back by suffering through the worse option. It just feels like waste if you don't 'use' it.
model: Spent is spent. Choose as if you were starting fresh today.
try_today: Pick one thing you keep only because it cost a lot (a gadget, a course, clothes). Ask: would I choose it today for free? Act on the answer.
try_team: List one project, club or plan your group keeps 'because we've put so much in'. Ask together: starting fresh today, would we pick it? Decide openly.

source.work: The Psychology of Sunk Cost (Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1985)

hook: Quitting feels like wasting it all. But is the waste already done?
title: Past Cost, Future Choice

steps.scenario: You're 2 years into guitar lessons your parents paid for. You've stopped enjoying it and want to try drawing instead. The thought 'all that money' stops you. You…

options.text: Ask: if I were choosing a hobby today, which would I pick?
options.feedback: Yes. The lessons are paid either way. Talk it through with your parents: the skills you built aren't lost, and the next hour is what's up for grabs.

options.text: Keep going so the money isn't wasted
options.feedback: A very human pull. But the money is spent whether you continue or not. More unhappy hours don't bring it back.

options.text: Quit everything at once, today
options.feedback: Clear-headed, but you can test it first: a month of drawing beside guitar shows what you actually prefer.

steps.scenario: Your group (a team at work, a club, a class project) is 18 months into a big plan. New numbers say it will likely fail even if finished. Someone says: 'We can't stop now, look how much we've put in.' You…

options.text: Compare the cost to finish with what it will likely earn
options.feedback: Right. Only future costs and gains decide. The 18 months are gone; the next 6 aren't. Say it kindly: stopping isn't the same as admitting failure.

options.text: Agree. Stopping would waste 18 months
options.feedback: Understandable, and common in groups and organisations. But finishing a plan that's likely to fail adds to the loss rather than rescuing what's spent.

options.text: Blame whoever started it
options.feedback: Tempting, but blame makes people defend past choices harder. In Staw's 1976 study, people who made the first call kept funding it more.

steps.scenario: You've spent £40 on skins in a game you're now bored of. A new season pass is £8. 'I've already spent so much on it,' you think. You…

options.text: Ask: if I'd never played, would I pay £8 for this today?
options.feedback: Yes. The £40 is gone either way. Only the next £8 is up for grabs.

options.text: Buy it so the skins aren't wasted
options.feedback: The skins already gave you fun. They can't vote on today's choice.

options.text: Uninstall in a rage right now
options.feedback: Maybe, but test it: a week off shows whether you miss it.

insight: Past costs pull us to keep going. The pull is real but modest in studies. And staying is fine when the future says so.
model: Ask 'From here, is this the best use of my next hour or next bit of money?' Ignore what's gone.
try_today: Pick one thing you're sticking with. Write one line: 'If I hadn't started yet, would I start today?' Act if the answer is a clear no.
try_team: Before your group reviews a long project (club, class or work), ban the phrase 'we've already invested'. Discuss only what's left to spend and the payoff.

source.work: Toward a Positive Theory of Consumer Choice (1980); Knee-deep in the Big Muddy (1976)

hook: Your project is 8 months in and wobbling. What may you count?
title: Kill or Keep: What Counts

game.prompt: Deciding whether to keep the project going. Should this count?

items.text: The 8 months the team has already put in
items.why: Gone whether you stop or go on. It feels heavy, but it can't change what happens next.

items.text: The 3 more months it needs to ship
items.why: Future cost. You pay it only if you keep going, so it belongs in the decision.

items.text: The setup fee you paid the vendor (no refunds)
items.why: Paid either way. Counting it is the classic sunk-cost slip.

items.text: The penalty for ending the contract early
items.why: You'd pay it only if you stop. A real future cost of quitting.

items.text: What testing taught you: clients skip the main feature
items.why: The money is sunk, but the lesson is live evidence about the future. Use it.

items.text: You backed this project hard in last quarter's review
items.why: Past pride, not future value. Wanting your first call to look right is a known driver of digging in.

insight: Verdict: count only what's still ahead. Spent time and fees are gone either way; lessons learned still count. A meta-analysis found feeling responsible for the first call makes digging in likelier.
model: Ask: if we hadn't started, would we start this today, with what we know now?
try_today: Pick one project you own. Write what it still costs and what it still could earn. Ignore what's already spent. Then decide.
try_team: In 5 minutes: name one ongoing project. Each person silently answers 'Would we start this today?' yes or no. Reveal together, then discuss only future costs.

source.work: Cleaning up the big muddy: A meta-analytic review of the determinants of escalation of commitment (Academy of Management Journal, 2012)

hook: Your team is full. A new 'quick' request lands. Who pays for it?
title: Every Yes Needs a 'Which No?'

steps.scenario: Your director asks your team to pilot a new reporting tool 'on the side'. The team is already at capacity. You reply…

options.text: "Happy to. Which of our current three priorities should slow down?"
options.feedback: Yes. You said yes and named the price. Now the trade-off is a choice made in the open, by the person who owns the priorities.

options.text: "Sure, we'll squeeze it in."
options.feedback: Kind and very common. The cost still gets paid, just quietly: late work, rushed quality or evenings. Nobody chose which.

options.text: "No, we're too busy."
options.feedback: It protects the team, which matters. But it can shut a good idea out. Naming the trade lets your director weigh it with you.

steps.scenario: In your 1:1, a strong report asks to join a big client project. They'd have to drop mentoring two new starters. You…

options.text: Back the move, but first plan who takes over the mentoring
options.feedback: Right. Growth for them is real value. So is the mentoring. Seeing what drops lets you cover it instead of losing it.

options.text: Say yes straight away: it's great for their career
options.feedback: Generous, and the career boost is real. The hidden cost is two new starters losing support without anyone deciding that.

options.text: Say no: the mentoring matters too much
options.feedback: Protecting new starters is a fair worry. But the 'no' has a price as well: a keen person's growth. Weigh both sides.

insight: Verdict: every yes spends time some other work needed. Studies find people weigh that hidden cost more when someone names it out loud.
model: Before any yes, ask: what is the best thing this will push out?
try_today: Next time you're asked to take something on, reply: 'Yes, if we pause X. Does that work?' Pick X before you answer.
try_team: 5 minutes: list everything the team is doing on a board. Each person marks one item they'd pause to make room for the next request. Compare marks.

source.work: Cost and Choice (1969); Opportunity Cost Consideration (Journal of Consumer Research, 2011)

hook: Ask adults about their biggest regret. One topic wins. Guess it.
title: Regret Lives Where Doors Were Open

game.question: Researchers pooled studies asking adults for their biggest life regret. School and education came top. What share of regrets was it?
game.explain: About 32% (Roese & Summerville, 2005). Next: career (22%) and romance (15%). Their idea: we regret most where we had the most chances. In school years, doors are wide open.

insight: Verdict: regret follows open doors, not just grades. Trying a club, a subject or a tryout costs little now, so skipped chances tend to linger. Mostly US adults studied.
model: Regret grows where chances were cheap. While a door is open, a small try costs less than a long 'what if'.
try_today: Pick one open door this week: a tryout, a club, a question to a teacher, a message to a mate. Do the smallest first bit.
try_team: With friends or class: each person writes one 'I'd be gutted if I never tried…' for this year. Swap papers and suggest one tiny first step.

source.work: What we regret most... and why (Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2005)
